html:
Decolonisation here means the end of European empires in Asia and Africa between 1945 and 1975, when most colonies became independent states. In those thirty years the number of sovereign states roughly tripled, and the United Nations grew from 51 members to well over a hundred.

It came then because the Second World War had drained Britain, France and the Netherlands, Japan's conquests had broken the image of European power in Asia, both the United States and the Soviet Union opposed the old empires, and nationalist movements had grown strong.

It came in waves:

  • 1945 to 1949: Asia. Indonesia declared independence in 1945 and won it from the Dutch in 1949; the Philippines followed in 1946, India and Pakistan in 1947 with the violence of Partition, and Burma and Ceylon in 1948.
  • 1954: France lost at Dien Bien Phu and left Indochina.
  • 1956 to 1962: North Africa, with Morocco, Tunisia and, after a long war, Algeria.
  • 1957 to 1968: sub-Saharan Africa, from Ghana in 1957 through the Year of Africa in 1960.
  • 1974 to 1975: after a revolution in Portugal, its African colonies became free.

Some handovers were peaceful; many were not, from Partition to the wars in Algeria, Kenya and Angola. Many new states tried to stay out of the Cold War through the Non-Aligned Movement. The story continues in the bars for independent African states and independent Southeast Asian states.
